Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) Requirement in ICH Nominations

solution.concept_anchor: No ceiling on multinational nomination co-nominators
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it invokes the World Heritage Convention's co-nomination rules — which do have practical limitations — and students familiar with that framework may apply it to the ICH context incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): There is no maximum limit on the number of co-nominating states for a multinational ICH nomination — unlike some other UNESCO frameworks.
Eliminate (b): The 1972 Convention's co-nomination practices impose practical (not strictly legal) limits; the 2003 Convention has no such constraint — applying 1972 rules to 2003 is a scope error.
Eliminate (c): Each co-nominating state must independently obtain FPIC from communities on its territory — Country J cannot substitute for Country K's community consent.
The 2003 Convention permits any number of states to co-nominate; each must obtain FPIC from its own communities; all receive inscription credit — option (d) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits knowledge of the 1972 World Heritage Convention's co-nomination norms. The 2003 Convention deliberately removed any ceiling on co-nominators to encourage international cultural solidarity and allow transnational practices to be nominated comprehensively. Students who apply 1972 principles to the 2003 framework — a scope-extension error — will select option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
A diplomatic scenario to apply the multinational nomination rules of the 2003 Convention.

The applicable principle: No ceiling on co-nominating states; each must demonstrate FPIC from its own communities; all receive inscription credit.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 2003 Convention imposes no maximum on the number of co-nominating states — any number may join.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 1972 Convention's co-nomination practices do not transfer to the 2003 framework — different rules apply.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Country J cannot satisfy FPIC on behalf of Country K's communities. FPIC is per community per territory — each state must independently demonstrate consent from communities on its soil.
• Option (d) — Correct: All 15 countries may co-nominate; each must independently obtain and document FPIC from communities on its territory; and each will receive inscription credit in its national count.

Value Addition:
• The strategic value of multinational nominations: each co-nominating state gets full inscription credit, encouraging broad coalitions.
• Nawrouz (12 co-nominators) is the largest multinational ICH nomination involving India.
• FPIC aggregation across multiple countries is a practical challenge — representative community bodies and religious councils are typically used.

concepts_used: Removal and De-inscription of ICH Elements — Article 35 and IGC Powers
Periodicity and Reporting Obligations of States Parties

solution.concept_anchor: Periodic reporting as IGC oversight tool for retention and removal
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who verify both A and R as true may default to (a) without separately testing whether R causally explains A's specific claim about the IGC's removal power.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? The IGC can remove an element if periodic reporting reveals it no longer meets inscription criteria — A is correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? State parties with elements on the RL must submit periodic reports every six years and on the USL every four years — R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R describes the reporting mechanism; A describes the IGC's removal power. R is a factually parallel statement about the reporting cycle but does not explain WHY the IGC has the power to remove — that power derives from the Convention text (Article 35 and IGC rules), not from the periodicity of reports. The reporting mechanism facilitates the exercise of removal power but is not its causal source.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT causally explain A — option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The ICH removal mechanism and the reporting obligation are both Convention features, but they are parallel instruments — not cause and effect.

Assertion (A): Correct — the IGC can, following the reporting mechanism, decide to retain, transfer, or remove an element if it no longer meets criteria. This power derives from the Convention and IGC's Rules of Procedure.

Reason (R): Correct — state parties must submit periodic reports: every six years for RL elements and every four years for USL elements.

Causal test: R does not explain A. The IGC's removal power is grounded in the Convention text and the mandate of the Committee — it would exist even without periodic reporting. Periodic reporting is the procedural mechanism through which the IGC is informed; it is not the source of the removal authority. The two are linked instrumentally but not causally.

Value Addition:
• No element has been formally de-inscribed from the RL as of 2024 — the removal power is theoretically important but practically unutilised.
• Elements have been transferred between RL and USL — a more commonly exercised adjustment.
• The IGC's decision to remove must follow the same consultation and due process principles as inscription decisions.

Criteria R.1–R.5 for Inscription on the Representative List

solution.concept_anchor: Register of Best Safeguarding Practices — third instrument

statement_analysis.statement: The Register of Best Safeguarding Practices recognises programmes, projects, and activities for the safeguarding of ICH that best reflect the principles and objectives of the 2003 Convention.
statement_analysis.reason: The Register is designed to identify and disseminate successful safeguarding models — it is the third instrument under the 2003 Convention alongside the RL and USL.

statement_analysis.statement: To be included in the Register of Best Safeguarding Practices, the programme or project must be from a country that already has at least one element inscribed on the Representative List.
statement_analysis.reason: No such precondition exists — the Register of Best Safeguarding Practices is open to any state party with a successful safeguarding programme, regardless of whether it has RL inscriptions.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2003 Convention establishes a fourth instrument called the 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' for elements facing imminent extinction — distinct from the Urgent Safeguarding List.
statement_analysis.reason: No such 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' exists in the 2003 Convention — this is a plausible fabrication; the Convention has exactly three instruments: RL, USL, and Register of Best Safeguarding Practices.

statement_analysis.statement: Programmes listed in the Register of Best Safeguarding Practices are shared internationally to promote their wider application in other countries.
statement_analysis.reason: The Register's explicit purpose is knowledge sharing and dissemination — successful safeguarding models are meant to be replicated and adapted by other states parties.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Reading the question: 'Only three' would mean three statements are correct. The strong distractor for students is Statement 3's plausible-fabrication 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' — it sounds sufficiently authoritative that students may mark it correct, raising their count to three.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Register recognises successful safeguarding programmes — correct.
Statement 2: No RL inscription precondition exists for Register entry — incorrect.
Statement 3: No 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' exists — this is a fabricated fourth instrument; incorrect.
Statement 4: Knowledge sharing and international dissemination is the Register's purpose — correct.
Two statements (1 and 4) are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the primary plausible-fabrication trap. The phrase 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' sounds like a logical extension of the USL for even more critically endangered elements. Students who have not specifically memorised that the 2003 Convention has exactly three instruments will treat this as a real fourth instrument and inflate their correct count. The 'fourth list' distractor is a classic UPSC device for this topic.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2003 Convention has exactly three instruments — no more. Any MCQ or statement introducing a 'fourth list' is a fabrication trap.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Register identifies best practices for safeguarding — it is the Convention's knowledge-sharing instrument.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No RL inscription precondition. Any state party with a proven safeguarding model can nominate it to the Register.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No 'Emergency Safeguarding Register' exists. Three instruments only: RL, USL, Register of Best Safeguarding Practices. This is a fabricated fourth instrument — the most common distractor for this concept area.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Dissemination and replication are the Register's core purposes.

Value Addition:
• The Register is the least discussed of the three instruments and appears most frequently as a distractor option in MCQs.
• India has not yet had a programme listed in the Register of Best Safeguarding Practices as of recent reporting.
• The three-instrument structure (RL, USL, Register) should be memorised as a complete set.
